title: Ephrem the Syrian
hookLine: the harp of the Spirit, who taught theology through hymns sung by women's choirs

lines: A TUNE GETS IN UNDER THE DOOR.
cards: Which do you remember better: the last sermon you heard, or the chorus of a song you haven't heard in years? A tune gets in under the door.

In the cities of Syria and Mesopotamia, in the early centuries of the church, there was a deacon who seems to have known that well. Rival teachers were spreading their ideas in catchy songs. He didn't ban the songs.
He wrote his own, and taught choirs of women to sing them. Syriac churches still sing hymns under his name.

teach.h: A DEACON WHO WROTE IN SYRIAC.
teach.b: Ephrem lived in Nisibis and later in Edessa, and wrote in Syriac, a form of Aramaic. Tradition calls him the harp of the Spirit.
He wrote sermons in verse and commentaries, but he's remembered for hymns: long, intricate songs with refrains, full of pictures. The poet Jacob of Serugh, writing after him, describes the choirs.

teach.h: HE GAVE THE WOMEN A VOICE.
teach.b: Ephrem saw that the women of the church had no voice in its teaching, so he gathered them into choirs and taught them his hymns, and they stood in the church and sang the faith aloud for everyone to hear.
The theology arrived on women's voices, set to tunes people could carry home. And what kind of theology?
Not definitions. Ephrem was wary of people who wanted to pin God down, to search out and measure what can't be measured. He used symbols instead.

A pearl, formed in the dark of the sea, becomes a picture of Christ. The world itself, he said in effect, is full of signs pointing to its maker, the way a scripture is. You don't trap the mystery in a sentence.

You circle it with images, and sing. Paul's letter to the Colossians, in the King James Bible, describes this kind of church: "teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs."

teach.h: PSALMS AND HYMNS AND SPIRITUAL SONGS.
teach.b: Tradition also says Ephrem cared for the sick and the hungry in a time of famine, and Orthodox, Catholic and Syriac churches alike honor him as a saint. In his churches, the faith wasn't only read. It was sung.

how: Syriac Christians still sing hymns attributed to Ephrem in their services, and Orthodox and Catholic Christians keep a feast day in his honor.

games.q: the harp of the spirit — tap the pairs.
p: a deacon who wrote hymns in Syriac
one of Ephrem's pictures of Christ

games.q: you're a deacon. rival teachers are spreading their ideas in catchy songs, and people are singing them in the streets. what do you do?
o: ban the songs and preach against them.
write a long book refuting them.
write songs of your own, and teach choirs of women to sing them.
games.why: Ephrem wrote hymns full of pictures and set choirs of women to sing them in church.

practice: Pick a tune you already know, a lullaby or a jingle, and one picture for something you believe or wonder about God, or what's holy: bread, light under a door, a pearl in the dark.
Hum the tune and fit a few of your own words to it; it needn't rhyme or be good. If you'd rather not sing, just hum, and hold the picture while you do.

wordCard.voice: Ephrem. A deacon and poet of Syria who taught the faith through hymns and images, sung by women's choirs. Tradition calls him the harp of the Spirit.

carryVoice: Your line: the harp of the spirit. A tune can carry what a definition can't. Until tomorrow.
